namingRules.description: A class or struct is named with a noun or noun phrase, PascalCase throughout, and carries no artificial type marker; skip prefixes like a leading 'C' that some older C++ conventions used.
namingRules.rationale: A PascalCase noun reads as the thing the type represents; a Hungarian-style prefix like 'C' is redundant since the declaration already states it is a class.
namingRules.sourceSection: Names of Classes, Structs, and Interfaces

namingRules.description: Interfaces are PascalCase adjectives or noun phrases carrying a capital 'I' at the front, and a class implementing one is usually named identically minus that leading 'I' (an interface ISerializer typically has a concrete implementation simply called Serializer).
namingRules.rationale: The 'I' prefix lets a reader distinguish an interface reference from a class reference at a glance, and keeps the interface/implementation pair visually linked.
namingRules.sourceSection: Names of Classes, Structs, and Interfaces

namingRules.description: A method's name is PascalCase and centers on a verb or verb phrase that names the action it carries out.
namingRules.rationale: Methods do something; a verb-led name makes call sites read like instructions rather than noun lookups.

namingRules.description: Properties take PascalCase names built from a noun, noun phrase, or adjective. A property backed by a collection should be pluralized on its own (Orders, not OrderList), and no property should share its exact name with a Get-prefixed method on the same type.
namingRules.rationale: Properties represent state, so noun-shaped names read naturally as 'object.Attribute'; a plural collection name avoids implying the property itself is a single item.

namingRules.description: A public or protected field gets the same PascalCase noun-phrase treatment as a property, with no scope-marking prefix tacked on (skip legacy conventions like a leading 'g' or 's' to flag global or static storage). Private and internal field casing is a choice this guideline leaves open.
namingRules.rationale: Public fields are part of the API surface and should follow the same PascalCase convention as properties and methods so the surface reads consistently.

namingRules.description: Choose a parameter name that describes what the value means, not what type it is, and use camelCase. The one carve-out is an operator-overload parameter that has no natural name of its own: use generic placeholders such as 'first'/'second' for a two-operand operator or 'operand' for a one-operand operator, rather than an abbreviation or a numbered index.
namingRules.rationale: A descriptive camelCase parameter name doubles as inline documentation at every call site that uses named arguments or shows IntelliSense.

namingRules.description: Namespaces are dot-separated PascalCase segments that generally widen from an organization identifier down to more specific areas, something like Organization, then a product or technology area, then an optional feature and sub-area, rather than mirroring an internal team or org-chart structure; a namespace should never reuse the exact name of a type defined within it, or vice versa.
namingRules.rationale: A company/product-rooted, PascalCase-dotted namespace avoids collisions across vendors and stays stable even when internal teams are reorganized.

namingRules.description: A plain enum type takes a singular PascalCase name; once it's marked with [Flags] so members can be OR-combined, switch to a plural PascalCase name instead.
namingRules.rationale: Singular vs. plural signals at the declaration whether a variable of that enum type holds exactly one value or a combinable set of values.
namingRules.sourceSection: Names of Classes, Structs, and Interfaces

namingRules.description: Skip appending words like 'Enum', 'Flag', or 'Flags' onto an enum type's own name; the enum keyword and an optional [Flags] attribute already make that clear without repeating it in the identifier.
namingRules.rationale: The suffix is redundant metadata the type system already expresses, and it makes names longer without adding information.
namingRules.sourceSection: Names of Classes, Structs, and Interfaces

namingRules.description: Enum members are PascalCase with no coded prefix tying them back to their containing enum; avoid an old-style abbreviation prefix the way some early COM-era APIs tagged every member of an enum with a short code.
namingRules.rationale: The member is always accessed through its enum type (EnumType.Member), so a per-member type prefix is redundant and adds noise.
namingRules.sourceSection: Names of Classes, Structs, and Interfaces

namingRules.description: A generic type parameter's name usually starts with a capital 'T' followed by something descriptive, and echoing a constraint it must satisfy is a good source for that description. When there's only one type parameter and its role is obvious from context, the bare letter 'T' on its own is acceptable.
namingRules.rationale: The 'T' prefix marks the identifier as a type parameter rather than an ordinary type name at a glance, while still allowing a descriptive name when a type has more than one parameter.
namingRules.sourceSection: Names of Classes, Structs, and Interfaces

namingRules.description: Name constants — both const fields and local constants — in PascalCase regardless of their access modifier, so public, internal, and private constants are all cased the same way.
namingRules.rationale: Keeping constant casing independent of visibility avoids a name having to change if its access modifier later changes, and keeps constants visually distinct from camelCase locals.
namingRules.sourceSection: C# identifier naming rules and conventions — Constants

namingRules.description: Local variables are camelCase with names clear enough that a reader doesn't have to guess their purpose; favor a few extra characters of clarity over brevity, except for a throwaway loop index where a single letter is fine.
namingRules.rationale: camelCase visually distinguishes a local variable from PascalCase types and members declared in the same scope, and a descriptive name reduces the need to trace a variable back to its declaration to understand it.
namingRules.sourceSection: C# identifier naming rules and conventions — Local variables

namingRules.description: State a boolean identifier's positive case rather than its negative one, preferring a name that reads true for the common, expected condition, and, when a prefix would clarify things further, common choices include forms like 'Is', 'Can', or 'Has'. As with any member, casing still follows whether it's a local (camelCase) or a public member (PascalCase).
namingRules.rationale: A negatively phrased boolean forces a double negative at every use site (e.g. '!NotConnected'), which is easy to misread; an affirmative name with an optional Is/Can/Has prefix reads directly as a yes/no question.
namingRules.sourceSection: Names of Type Members; C# identifier naming rules and conventions

namingRules.description: Skip Hungarian-notation prefixes that spell out a variable's type in miniature (things like 'str', 'i', or 'b' tacked onto the front of a name), and don't rely on underscores or other punctuation to break up words inside an identifier.
namingRules.rationale: Modern tooling shows a variable's declared type on hover, so an encoded type prefix only adds clutter and can go stale if the type changes; PascalCase/camelCase word boundaries already remove the need for separators.

commentRules.triggerCondition: A class, struct, interface, or enum is declared with public or protected visibility.
commentRules.description: Give every publicly visible type an XML doc comment with at least a <summary> element describing what it represents; documenting private types is optional.
commentRules.sourceSection: Recommended XML documentation comment tags — General tags

commentRules.triggerCondition: A public or protected method is declared; a <param> element is expected for each declared parameter, and a <returns> element is expected when the method's return type is not void.
commentRules.description: Document every public/protected method with a <summary>, one <param> tag per parameter, and a <returns> tag describing the return value when the method returns one; the C# compiler warns when a method's <param> tags do not match its actual parameter list.
commentRules.sourceSection: Recommended XML documentation comment tags — Member tags

commentRules.triggerCondition: A public or protected property is declared.
commentRules.description: Document every public/protected property with a <summary>, and add a <value> element describing what the property represents; Visual Studio's generated property doc template includes <value> by default.
commentRules.sourceSection: Recommended XML documentation comment tags — Member tags

commentRules.triggerCondition: A public generic type or generic method declares one or more type parameters.
commentRules.description: Document each type parameter of a public generic type or method with a <typeparam name="..."> element; the compiler verifies that documented type-parameter names match the declaration.
commentRules.sourceSection: Recommended XML documentation comment tags — Generic type documentation

commentRules.triggerCondition: A public/protected method throws an exception as part of its documented, expected contract (e.g., it validates an argument and throws on failure).
commentRules.description: Where a public/protected method can throw an exception as part of its contract, add an <exception cref="..."> element naming the exception type and describing the condition that triggers it.
commentRules.sourceSection: Recommended XML documentation comment tags — Member tags

commentRules.triggerCondition: A member of a publicly visible enum type is declared.
commentRules.description: Give each member of a publicly visible enum its own <summary> XML doc comment describing what that value represents, consistent with the general guidance to document all publicly visible types and members.
commentRules.sourceSection: Recommended XML documentation comment tags — When to apply XML documentation comments

coverageGaps: The Framework Design Guidelines hub and its sub-pages focus on the public API surface; local-variable, private-field, and constant casing are not addressed there and were instead sourced from the companion C# 'Identifier names — rules and conventions' page.

The 'Names of Type Members' field guidance is explicitly scoped to public/protected static fields; private/internal field casing (e.g. '_camelCase', 's_' prefixes) is a separate, newer C#-style convention, not a Framework Design Guidelines rule, so no conflict is implied between the two field rules.

Boolean-identifier prefixes ('Is'/'Can'/'Has') are only ever framed as 'Consider... where it adds value' — the guidelines give no crisp rule for when a prefix is required versus when the bare affirmative name is preferred.

Type/suffix pairing rules for classes derived from specific base types (e.g. 'Exception', 'Attribute', 'EventArgs', 'Collection', 'Dictionary', 'Stream', 'Permission' suffixes, and delegate suffixes 'EventHandler'/'Callback') exist on the Classes/Structs/Interfaces page but were left out to stay within the target rule count — they are narrow, base-type-specific sub-cases of the general class-naming rule rather than a distinct identifier kind.
There is no dedicated 'Names of Constants' page; constant PascalCase guidance was found only on the separate C# coding-style 'Identifier names' page, not within the naming-guidelines hub tree itself.

The recommended-XML-tags page does not use Do/Consider/Avoid/Do-not severity language the way the Framework Design Guidelines pages do, so CommentRule severities here are inferred from its 'required' vs. 'recommended' wording rather than mapped from those exact labels.
No explicit, enumerable list of 'widely accepted' acronyms is given (only examples like IO, UI, Id, Xml) — judging an acronym as acceptable is left to reviewer discretion.
